subject: feminism
title: The Modern Women's Foundation (現代婦女基金會): Taiwan's first women's protection center and the laws it built
dek: Founded in 1987 by Taipei City councilor Pan Wei-kang, Modern Women's Foundation became Taiwan's first organization dedicated to protecting women from sexual assault, domestic violence and sexual harassment when those crimes had no legal framework and police would not take reports. It drafted or co-drafted four major laws between 1997 and 2005, including Asia's first domestic violence prevention act, and continues to serve more than 8,000 victims each year. This lesson explains what a protection center does, how it differs from an advocacy organization, how Taiwan's charity transparency laws work, and what a vintage shop partnership could mean.
era: 1987 to the present: founding in May 1987 about two and a half months before martial law was lifted in July, the 1988 Women's Guardian Center, the law-drafting campaigns of the 1990s after Deng Ru-wen's case and Peng Wan-ru's murder, the 2001 national 113 hotline, court service centers and professional services after 2002, and today's work against dating violence and stalking
honesty: This lesson is text only. The history comes from Modern Women's Foundation's own English and Chinese pages, the Ministry of Health and Welfare's 113 hotline history, Wikipedia articles on Deng Ru-wen's case and Peng Wan-ru, the Taipei Times and other news sources, Taiwan legal databases for the Foundations Act and Charity Fundraising Act, and the earlier lessons on Taiwan's women's movement, Awakening Foundation and Garden of Hope. The eight-thousand-victims-per-year figure and the three-thousand-families figure come from the foundation's English introduction. I did not find publicly accessible recent financial reports with detailed breakdowns on the foundation's website during research, so this lesson describes the legal framework for transparency rather than specific dollar figures. Where a claim rests only on the foundation's own pages or where legal obligations leave room for interpretation, the lesson says so. This is a study guide, not legal or partnership advice: before cool dairy signs anything, confirm the details with the organization and, if needed, an accountant or lawyer.

timeline.label: Foundation established
timeline.detail: Pan Wei-kang, then a Taipei City councilor, and a group of advocates establish Modern Women's Foundation on 1 May 1987, about two and a half months before martial law was lifted on 15 July. The original mission is to help women balance traditional and modern roles.

timeline.label: Women's Guardian Center
timeline.detail: Realizing that women lack even basic safety protections, the foundation opens Taiwan's first Women's Guardian Center (婦女護衛中心), offering legal, medical and police-accompaniment services to victims of sexual assault, domestic violence and sexual harassment.

timeline.label: Deng Ru-wen case
timeline.detail: In October 1993, Deng Ru-wen kills her abusive husband after years of violence. Her case, defended by lawyer Wang Ju-hsuan, exposes the absence of domestic violence laws and galvanizes women's groups, including Modern Women's Foundation, to draft legislation.

timeline.label: Peng Wan-ru murdered; drafting resumes
timeline.detail: DPP Women's Affairs Department director Peng Wan-ru is raped and murdered in Kaohsiung on 30 November 1996. Her death reignites public outrage over women's safety. Pan Wei-kang discovers judge Kao Feng-hsian has completed a domestic violence bill draft and uses her legislative position to advance it.

timeline.label: Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act
timeline.detail: Taiwan enacts the Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act on 22 January 1997, establishing prevention centers, victim services, offender treatment and a national registry. Modern Women's Foundation co-drafted the bill, commissioning police college lecturer Liao Shu-wen to write the draft.

timeline.label: Domestic Violence Prevention Act
timeline.detail: Taiwan enacts the Domestic Violence Prevention Act on 24 June 1998, becoming Asia's first country with a civil protection order system for domestic violence. Modern Women's Foundation's drafting committee, led by judge Kao Feng-hsian, wrote the bill. The act takes effect in 1999.

timeline.label: Criminal Code amendment
timeline.detail: Legislator Pan Wei-kang leads the amendment of Criminal Code Chapter 16, which moves sexual assault crimes from 'offenses against morality' to a new chapter on 'offenses against sexual autonomy,' changing the legal frame from public decency to personal rights and making marital rape a crime.

timeline.label: 113 protection hotline established
timeline.detail: On 13 January 2001, the Ministry of the Interior consolidates earlier hotlines into the 113 protection hotline, a 24-hour national service for domestic violence, sexual assault and child protection. It is run by the government, not by Modern Women's Foundation.

timeline.label: Court service centers
timeline.detail: Modern Women's Foundation establishes Taiwan's first family-violence service center inside Shilin District Court, with social workers helping victims file protection orders, access legal advice and connect to welfare resources. The model spreads nationwide.

timeline.label: Sexual Harassment Prevention Act
timeline.detail: Modern Women's Foundation proposes a Sexual Harassment Prevention Act to cover harassment in public spaces not addressed by workplace or school laws. The act was promulgated on 5 February 2005 and took effect one year later, on 5 February 2006.

timeline.label: Sexual assault law reform
timeline.detail: Modern Women's Foundation, with board member Lai Fang-yu leading a team that included former CEO Lin Mei-hsun, Wang Ju-hsuan and others, pushes amendments to the Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act protecting child victims' court rights, establishing expert witnesses and banning unauthorized sharing of victim information.

timeline.label: Trauma recovery center
timeline.detail: The foundation opens a sexual-assault trauma recovery center (展心性侵害創傷復原中心) to support long-term healing after the immediate crisis ends.

timeline.label: 'Only YES means YES' campaign
timeline.detail: Modern Women's Foundation launches its 'Only YES means YES — without consent, it is sexual assault' public education campaign, winning a Taiwan public relations award.

timeline.label: Stalking and Harassment Prevention Act
timeline.detail: After years of advocacy by women's groups including Modern Women's Foundation, Taiwan passes the Stalking and Harassment Prevention Act in November 2021. It takes effect in June 2022, criminalizing repeated sex- or gender-related stalking and harassment.

sections.title: Before the laws: when police refused to take reports

blocks.text: In 1987, when Modern Women's Foundation was established in May, Taiwan was still under martial law, which would not be lifted until 15 July of that year. Women had gained the right to vote decades earlier, but the legal system offered almost no protection against violence inside the home or in intimate relationships. A husband beating a wife was considered a family matter. A woman reporting sexual assault faced police who might refuse to take her statement, doctors who might refuse to treat her, and a legal code that classified rape as an offense against public morality rather than against her person.

The foundation's English-language history describes what victims faced: 'police did not accept their cases, medical professionals refused to treat them, and there were no other governmental services provided to assist them.' If a man beat a woman on the street and a bystander intervened, he could say 'she is my wife' and the bystander would walk away. The assumption was that she must have done something wrong, or had an affair, to deserve it.

This was the gap Modern Women's Foundation set out to fill: not only advocacy and law reform, which groups like Awakening Foundation were already doing, but direct services to women whose safety was in immediate danger and who had nowhere else to turn.

sections.title: 1987 to 1988: from general rights to urgent protection

blocks.text: Pan Wei-kang (潘維剛), then a Taipei City councilor, founded Modern Women's Foundation in May 1987 with a group of people committed to women's rights. The foundation's original purpose, according to its own account, was to help women navigate the balance between traditional and modern roles. But as soon as they began working, they discovered that many women could not even think about balancing roles because they were not safe.

In 1988 the foundation opened the Women's Guardian Center (婦女護衛中心), Taiwan's first center dedicated to protecting women and children from sexual assault, domestic violence and sexual harassment. The center brought together lawyers, crime-prevention experts, doctors and social workers to provide what the state would not: legal advice, accompaniment to medical appointments and police interviews, and other emergency services. It was the first organization in Taiwan to do this work, and it had to invent the model as it went.

Pan Wei-kang's own political career gave the foundation unusual leverage. She served as a legislator from 1993 to 2002 and again from 2005 to 2016, always on the Kuomintang ticket. That let her draft bills, lobby colleagues and push for passage from inside the legislature. The combination of direct service and legislative power is rare. Most organizations do one or the other. Modern Women's Foundation did both.

sections.kicker: The cases that changed the law
sections.title: Deng Ru-wen and Peng Wan-ru: two tragedies that made reform urgent

blocks.text: Two events in the 1990s turned the Women's Guardian Center's quiet case-by-case work into a national legislative campaign.

The first was the 1993 case of Deng Ru-wen (鄧如雯). Deng had been raped by Lin A-chi, forced to marry him after she became pregnant, and beaten throughout the marriage. Lin also assaulted Deng's family, including attempting to rape her sister and threatening her siblings. On 27 October 1993, after years of abuse and threats to kill her family, Deng killed Lin while he slept. She immediately called the police and turned herself in.

Deng's trial became a referendum on how Taiwan treated domestic violence. Women's groups, including Awakening Foundation and Modern Women's Foundation, rallied to her defense. Lawyer Wang Ju-hsuan (王如玄), retained through the DPP, argued that Deng had been in a state of mental exhaustion from prolonged abuse. After an initial sentence of five years and six months, the High Court reduced it to three years on 2 August 1994, accepting the argument of diminished capacity. Deng was imprisoned on 19 April 1995 and paroled in March 1996, having served less than a year in prison following about nine months of pretrial custody.

The case exposed the absence of any legal framework for domestic violence. Deng had tried to leave, had reported to police, and had been forced back by Lin's escalating violence. The system had no tools to protect her except after she had already killed her abuser. In 1994, women's groups led by Awakening Foundation began meeting with then-Justice Minister Ma Ying-jeou to discuss drafting a domestic violence law. The Interior Ministry provided one million New Taiwan dollars to Awakening Foundation for research. Progress was slow.

The second event was the murder of Peng Wan-ru (彭婉如) on 30 November 1996. Peng was the director of the Democratic Progressive Party's Women's Affairs Department and a well-known feminist. She disappeared in Kaohsiung the night before a DPP convention after getting into a taxi. Her body was found three days later outside an abandoned warehouse with more than thirty stab wounds. She had been raped. The murder was never solved.

Peng's death produced nationwide outrage. The DPP convention she had been attending passed her proposal to reserve one-quarter of party seats for women. Women's groups organized a massive march in December 1996. Modern Women's Foundation, led by Pan Wei-kang, realized that judge Kao Feng-hsian (高鳳仙) had already completed a draft domestic violence bill based on United States and New Zealand laws. Pan used her position in the legislature to push the bill forward. It was introduced in July 1996, before Peng's death, but her murder gave it unstoppable momentum.

sections.title: Four laws in eight years: the legislative record

blocks.text: Modern Women's Foundation co-drafted or drafted four major laws between 1997 and 2005. Each one filled a gap the earlier system had left open.

The Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act was promulgated on 22 January 1997. Modern Women's Foundation commissioned Liao Shu-wen (廖書雯), a lecturer at Taiwan Police College, to draft the bill. It established sexual assault prevention centers in every city and county, required coordination among police, medical, social-service and education agencies, mandated prevention education in schools, set up a national offender registry, and created victim services including accompaniment, counseling and legal aid. Before this law, sexual assault victims had nowhere to go for coordinated help. After it, every local government had to provide a center.

The Domestic Violence Prevention Act was promulgated on 24 June 1998 and took effect in 1999. Taiwan became Asia's first country to have a civil protection order system for domestic violence. The act defined domestic violence broadly, covering physical, psychological and economic abuse between family members, spouses and cohabitants. It allowed courts to issue emergency, temporary and long-term protection orders that could bar an abuser from the home, require them to stay a set distance away, and mandate counseling or treatment. It also created family-violence service centers and a mandatory reporting system. Judge Kao Feng-hsian led the drafting committee, which Modern Women's Foundation had set up in 1996.

The Criminal Code amendment of 1999, pushed through the legislature by Pan Wei-kang, restructured how Taiwan's legal system understood rape. Before 1999, sexual offenses sat in a chapter called 'offenses against morality' (妨害風化), which treated rape as a public-decency crime rather than a violation of a person's autonomy. The amendment created a new chapter, 'offenses against sexual autonomy' (妨害性自主), and made clear that forced sex was a crime against the victim's will, not against society's sense of propriety. The reform also changed rape from a complaint-only offense to a public offense and explicitly recognized that a husband could rape his wife, which earlier interpretations had left unclear.

The Sexual Harassment Prevention Act of 2005 was the last of the four. The Gender Equality in Employment Act and the Gender Equity Education Act already covered harassment at work and in schools, but public spaces had no protection. Modern Women's Foundation proposed a bill to close that gap. The Sexual Harassment Prevention Act was promulgated on 5 February 2005 and took effect one year later, on 5 February 2006, covering harassment in any setting not addressed by the other two laws and setting up complaint and investigation procedures.

After 2005, the foundation continued to push for amendments. In 2015 it worked with a team of lawyers to reform the Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act again, adding protections for child victims in court, establishing expert witnesses for child and disability cases, and banning anyone from sharing information that could identify a victim. In 2021, after years of advocacy by many women's groups, Taiwan passed the Stalking and Harassment Prevention Act, which Modern Women's Foundation had supported. It took effect in June 2022.

sections.title: What a protection center does: from hotlines to court social workers

blocks.text: The foundation's English introduction says it assists more than 8,000 victims of domestic violence, sexual assault and sexual harassment each year, and also helps nearly 3,000 high-conflict families in the courts each year. Those are large numbers, close to Garden of Hope's scale in some areas, and they reflect a service model built around crisis response and legal accompaniment rather than long-term residential care.

The core services include twenty-four-hour hotlines, emergency shelter referrals, hospital and police accompaniment, legal advice, court support and counseling. In 2002 Modern Women's Foundation established Taiwan's first family-violence service center inside Shilin District Court in Taipei. Social workers stationed at the court help victims file protection orders, understand legal procedures, access welfare resources and find safe housing. The model spread to other courts around Taiwan, and by 2013 the foundation was operating service centers in Taipei, Taichung, Hsinchu and Hualien district courts.

The foundation also runs programs for populations that face extra barriers: intimate-partner violence among LGBTQ couples, which it began addressing in 2009 in partnership with the Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association; and dating violence among teenagers, which it has worked on since 2008. In 2016 it launched an education campaign aimed at young people and set up a website, 戀愛乾麻醬, to help teenagers learn about healthy relationships.

In 2017 the foundation opened a sexual-assault trauma recovery center (展心性侵害創傷復原中心) to provide longer-term support after the crisis phase. That same year it expanded services in Hualien and Hsinchu to include children who witness domestic violence, recognizing that those children are also victims even if they are not directly harmed.

This is a different model from Garden of Hope's network of shelters and long-term residential programs, and different again from Awakening Foundation's law-reform and hotline work. Modern Women's Foundation sits in between: it provides direct crisis services, but the services are built to get people through the legal and medical systems rather than to house them for months. It also continues to draft and lobby for laws, but its main identity is as a protection center, not a policy think tank.

sections.title: How Taiwan's laws require foundations to report

blocks.text: Two laws govern how Taiwan's foundations and charities must disclose their finances and activities: the Foundations Act of 2018 (財團法人法) and the Charity Fundraising Act (公益勸募條例).

The Foundations Act requires every foundation to submit its annual work plan and budget to the supervising authority within one month of the start of the year, and its work report and financial statements within five months of year-end. Foundations above a certain size must have their financial statements audited by a certified public accountant. Those documents must then be publicly disclosed within one month after they are filed with the authority for the record. Foundations must also disclose a list of donors and recipients from the previous year, including names and amounts, unless a donor or recipient objects in writing in advance, or disclosure would hinder or seriously affect operations, and the competent authority agrees. Disclosure can be by newspaper, website or public inspection. Foundations that fail to comply face fines of NT$30,000 to NT$150,000.

The Charity Fundraising Act applies to specific fundraising campaigns rather than to general operations. Any organization that conducts a public fundraising drive must report the campaign results to the supervising authority within thirty days after the campaign period ends, including a list of donors, total funds raised and an income-and-expenditure report. The organization must also publicly disclose that information. Separately, when the funds are spent, the organization must file a completion report within thirty days after the use plan is completed, showing how the money was used, with outcome data and receipts. The deadline for the completion report can be extended by up to thirty days if needed. The government maintains a public online system where anyone can look up a campaign's permit, see whether reports are overdue, and read past performance.

Modern Women's Foundation lists annual reports and financial audit reports on its website under a section called '財務簽證報告' (audited financial reports). The reports are organized by year, with the most recent covering 2025 (民國114年). The foundation's legal name is 財團法人現代婦女教育基金會, and its tax ID is 76904597. Until 2015, it published combined reports with a separate Taipei-based entity, 財團法人台北市現代婦女基金會, which handled Taipei-specific services. Since then the reports have covered the main foundation's nationwide work.

Because I could not access detailed recent financial statements during this research, this lesson cannot provide specific income, spending or reserve figures the way the Awakening Foundation lesson did. What it can say is that the law requires those figures to exist, to be audited and to be published. A potential partner such as cool dairy should ask for the most recent audited financial statement, the breakdown of income by source, the ratio of program spending to administrative overhead, and an explanation of any large changes from year to year.

sections.title: How a shop could partner transparently

blocks.text: If cool dairy wants to donate proceeds to Modern Women's Foundation, there are several standard models used by Taiwan shops and brands.

items: Percentage of sales: the shop commits to donating a fixed percentage of revenue from all sales, or from a specific product line, during a set period. Example: 'Five percent of every purchase in November 2026 goes to Modern Women's Foundation.' This model requires the shop to keep clear sales records and issue a single donation at the end of the period.

Lump-sum donation with storytelling: the shop donates a fixed amount up front and tells customers that their purchases supported that donation. Example: 'cool dairy donated NT$50,000 to Modern Women's Foundation this quarter. Your support made that possible.' This is simpler to execute and report, and it avoids the complexity of tying individual transactions to charity.

Product-specific partnership: the shop sells a co-branded item or a limited-edition piece and donates all or part of the profit. Example: a tote bag designed with the foundation's input, where the proceeds after costs go to the organization. This works well for items that can carry a message or tell a story.

Invoice donation code: Taiwan's electronic invoice system lets customers donate their receipt's lottery chance to a registered charity by entering a 'love code' (愛心碼). The shop can print the foundation's code on receipts or packaging. The foundation's website would list its code, or cool dairy can ask for it. This is a zero-cost way to let customers give directly without requiring the shop to collect and forward money.

blocks.text: Whichever model cool dairy chooses, transparency means documenting the partnership in writing, keeping receipts, getting a donation receipt from the foundation, and publishing the total donated and when. Under the Charity Fundraising Act, if the shop's campaign counts as public fundraising—meaning it publicly solicits money tied to a cause—cool dairy would need to apply for a permit and file reports. However, only public schools, administrative legal persons, public-interest associations, and foundations may obtain fundraising permits under the Act; a for-profit shop cannot. If cool dairy wants to publicly solicit donations, it must do so under Modern Women's Foundation's own permitted campaign. If the shop is simply donating its own revenue and telling customers about it afterward, that is not public fundraising and requires no permit. The distinction matters. Before launching, cool dairy should confirm with the foundation and, if needed, a lawyer which model applies.

Modern Women's Foundation, like other established organizations, likely has standard partnership agreements and knows which models require permits. The first step is to ask. The second step is to be clear with customers: tell them exactly how much will be donated, when, to whom, and for what. The third step is to follow through and report the outcome.

sections.title: Modern Women's Foundation, Garden of Hope and Awakening: three models

blocks.text: The three organizations covered so far in this series—Awakening Foundation, Garden of Hope Foundation and Modern Women's Foundation—represent three different approaches to women's rights work, and understanding the differences helps clarify what a donation supports.

Awakening Foundation is mainly an advocacy and watchdog organization. Its total income in 2025 was about NT$5.7 million. It has six or seven paid staff. Its products are draft bills, policy reports, lobby campaigns, volunteer trainings and public pressure. It does run a family-law advice hotline, but most of its work is aimed at changing systems rather than helping individuals through them.

Garden of Hope Foundation is mainly a service provider, and a large one. Its total income in 2025 was about NT$640.7 million. It runs shelters, halfway houses, employment programs and counseling centers across Taiwan, many under government contracts. It also advocates for laws and policies, but its identity is as an organization that operates facilities and delivers long-term case management. Its scale is more than a hundred times Awakening's.

Modern Women's Foundation is both: it provides crisis services to thousands of victims each year, and it drafts laws. Its scale is closer to Garden of Hope's in service numbers, though its income is likely smaller because its services are shorter-term and often embedded in courts and hospitals rather than in residential centers it owns. It also retains the legislative access that Pan Wei-kang brought when she founded it, even though she is no longer in the legislature. This dual identity—service provider and lawmaker—is unusual.

For a shop like cool dairy, the choice among them is not about which is better but about what story the shop wants to tell. Supporting Awakening means supporting the people who write the laws. Supporting Garden of Hope means supporting shelters and long-term care. Supporting Modern Women's Foundation means supporting the organizations that stand between a victim and the police station, the hospital and the courthouse, at the moment of crisis, and that also built the legal tools those institutions now use.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Modern Women's Foundation helped draft the laws that created Taiwan's domestic violence protection system, and it pioneered court service centers that it still operates today. Should a donor give to the organization that built the legal framework, even if the government now enforces those laws and runs national hotlines? Or should the donor only support work the organization still directly controls, like the court centers and crisis services it continues to provide?

fun_fact.title: The foundation's two names and the separated histories
fun_fact.text: Until around 2015, Modern Women's Foundation published combined financial reports with a separate Taipei-based foundation called 財團法人台北市現代婦女基金會. The two shared an office and worked closely together, but they were separate legal entities with separate budgets. The national foundation, 財團法人現代婦女教育基金會, handled nationwide advocacy and services; the Taipei foundation focused on local Taipei programs. This structure let the organizations divide labor and access different funding sources. Since 2015, the reports published on the website cover only the national foundation's work, though the earlier combined reports are still available in the archive. This is the kind of organizational detail that sounds boring but matters a great deal when reading financial statements or signing a partnership: which entity are you actually dealing with?
